subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

periods.activity_title: Shopping at the Market: Costs, Change, and Currency

tasks_in_class.description: Find costs for different quantities of fruits/vegetables; find what combinations sum to ₹163 (more than one possibility).
Lou and Daisy buy 3 kg bananas (₹165). Which of the currency options a–e can they use to pay?

homework.description: Complete 9 Cost–Paid–Balance grids by finding the missing value in each row.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the market price list from the Mawlynnong trip story. Distribute play-money notes and coins. Pairs use the price list to compute what different quantities of fruits and vegetables cost, building a feel for rupee amounts.

Let Us Do, p.97 ("find combinations of items that sum to ₹163...."). Children use the price list, choose items, add their prices and check whether the total reaches ₹163. Emphasise that more than one combination is valid; pairs share at least two different solutions with the class.

Let Us Do, p.98 ("which currency options can be used to pay ₹165...."). Children examine options a–e, test each against ₹165 using play money, and state which are valid. Class discusses why some options fall short or are awkward.
Brief whole-class discussion: what strategies helped find the ₹163 combinations quickly? Introduce the Cost–Paid–Balance grid format as homework (Let Us Do, p.98).

periods.teacher_notes: When children find combinations for ₹163, prompt them to record each combination in a list before trying another — this prevents re-counting the same one. A common error is treating 'can be used to pay ₹165' as 'sums exactly to ₹165'; remind children that giving more than ₹165 and receiving change is also valid.
materials: Price list chart (written on the board or a sheet)

section_titles: A Strange Puzzle — Change from Oranges
periods.activity_title: Change in Your Pocket and a Triangle of Numbers

tasks_in_class.description: Find the balance (paid amount minus ₹42) for Krishna (₹50), Sudama (₹100), Mala (₹200), and Neela (₹500).
Place numbers 1–6 in triangle nodes so that the sum on each side is 9. No numbers repeated.
What other sums can you make with these 6 numbers? Can you make 12 on each side? Can you make 13?

homework.description: Use same numbers 1–6 and arrange so that the sum on each side of the triangle is 10.

time_bands.activity: Read the rhyming puzzle aloud together. A Strange Puzzle!, p.99 ("find balance for Krishna, Sudama, Mala, Neela...."). Children individually subtract ₹42 from each note value, writing each step in columns. Pairs compare answers and check by adding the change back to ₹42.

Draw a triangle with six nodes (3 vertices, 3 midpoints) on the board. Let Us Play, p.100 ("place numbers 1–6 so each side sums to 9...."). Distribute numbered slips 1–6 per pair. Pairs arrange slips in the triangle, add each side, and adjust until all three sides equal 9. Share one working arrangement with the class.

Let Us Play, p.100 ("what other sums can you make? Can you make 12? Can you make 13?..."). Groups record which target sums are achievable and report findings. Guide a short class discussion: are some targets impossible? How do children know?
Set homework: Let Us Play, p.100 — arrange the same six numbers so each side sums to 10.

periods.teacher_notes: For the change puzzle, a common error is subtracting ₹21 instead of ₹42 (the cost of two oranges); ask children to re-read what each child bought before subtracting. For the Magic Triangle, encourage systematic placement — try putting the largest numbers at the midpoints first — rather than random guessing.
materials: Numbered slips 1–6 (one set per pair, cut from paper)

periods.activity_title: Blocks, Bundles, and the Carrying Column

tasks_in_class.description: Estimate the number of teachers going on the trip (24 + 28) before computing.
Estimate the number of children going on the trip (438 + 476) before computing.
38 + 16: estimate the money spent on pusaw, then write the final answer after regrouping in the H-T-O boxes.
185 + 125: estimate the trip money, then write the final answer after regrouping in the H-T-O boxes.

time_bands.activity: Display Dienes blocks (or draw them) for ones, tens, and hundreds. Ask children to represent a 2-digit number with blocks and read it aloud. This grounds the H-T-O language before any adding begins.

Add Up, p.101 ("estimate teachers going on the trip: 24 + 28....") and Add Up, p.102 ("estimate children on the trip: 438 + 476...."). For each, children write an estimate first, then use block diagrams to add, regrouping ones into tens and tens into hundreds. Discuss how the estimate compares with the exact answer.

Add Up, p.103 ("estimate and solve 38 + 16 in H-T-O boxes...."). Model the column layout on the board with H, T, O headers. Children write the estimate, then complete the column addition with regrouping. Repeat for Add Up, p.104 ("estimate and solve 185 + 125....") with a 3-digit example.

Whole-class check: a child explains each regrouping step in their own words. Ask: 'Why does a 1 appear above the tens column?' Consolidate the idea that 10 ones become 1 ten, and 10 tens become 1 hundred.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent error at the regrouping step is writing both digits of a two-digit sum in the same column (e.g. writing '14' under the ones column instead of recording 4 and carrying 1). Demonstrating with actual blocks that 14 ones must be exchanged for 1 ten and 4 ones makes this concrete. Estimation also guards against this error — if the estimate is about 50 and the student gets 114, they recognise something went wrong.
materials: Dienes blocks or token sets (ones, tens, hundreds per pair)
H-T-O grid drawn on the board

periods.activity_title: Tables, Columns, and a School Story

tasks_in_class.description: Complete the Kalakshitij table: find total boys, total girls, total tabla players, and total singers.
Preeti's school has 423 children; cousin's school has 178 more. How many children study in Preeti's cousin's school?

homework.book_ref: Let Us Do Q1 follow-up, p.105
homework.description: 15 more girls join to play tabla. How many girls play tabla now?

time_bands.activity: Let Us Do Q1, p.105 ("complete the Kalakshitij table: total boys, girls, tabla players, singers...."). Children read the table, identify which cells are missing, and add the given numbers in columns. Discuss how row-totals and column-totals provide a cross-check.

Let Us Do Q2, p.105 ("add by aligning in columns: 32+47, 654+95, 286+123, 476+324, 700+289, 534+483...."). Children work independently, aligning digits in H-T-O columns, regrouping where needed. Circulate and check that carrying marks are placed above the correct column.

Let Us Do Q3, p.105 ("Preeti's school has 423 children; cousin's school has 178 more...."). Children translate the word problem into a column addition, estimate first, then compute. One child writes and explains the solution on the board.
Set homework: Let Us Do Q1 follow-up, p.105 — 15 more girls join to play tabla; find the new total.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often misalign digits when one addend has fewer digits than the other (e.g. 654+95); stress right-alignment under the ones column before adding. The Kalakshitij table cross-check — row sums must equal the grand total, column sums must also equal it — is a powerful self-verification habit worth establishing here.
materials: Board and chalk/marker for column-addition demonstration

periods.activity_title: Breaking Tens and Hundreds: Regrouping to Subtract

tasks_in_class.description: Estimate the difference: how many more children bought Pusaw than fruit plates (83 − 46)?
Estimate how many children are waiting to visit the Living Roots Bridge (438 − 215).
Ram Chacha: 527 mangoes this year, 264 last year. Estimate then find how many more mangoes this year; use/draw tokens.
Subtract by aligning in columns: (a) 83−29 (b) 345−123 (c) 763−437 (d) 803−350 (e) 900−328.

homework.description: Ranganna made 639 dolls, sold 531. Estimate then find how many dolls are left; use/draw tokens.

time_bands.activity: Subtract It, p.106 ("estimate the difference: 83 − 46 and 438 − 215...."). Children write estimates (round to nearest ten), then confirm the direction: is the answer closer to 30 or to 50? This checks reasonableness before the column algorithm.

Model 83 − 46 with Dienes blocks on the board: show that 3 ones are not enough to subtract 6, so regroup 1 ten into 10 ones. Record each step in the H-T-O column. Repeat with 438 − 215 and then one example with a zero digit (e.g. a preparation for 803-type problems). Children copy and annotate each step.

Let Us Solve, p.108 ("Ram Chacha: 527 mangoes this year, 264 last year; find how many more...."). Children draw or use token diagrams, estimate first, then apply the column algorithm. Emphasise the word 'regrouping', not 'borrowing'.

Let Us Solve Q5, p.109 ("subtract in columns: 83−29, 345−123, 763−437, 803−350, 900−328...."). Children work independently on the five items. Set Let Us Solve Q4, p.108 (Ranganna's dolls) as homework.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error in subtraction with regrouping is subtracting the smaller digit from the larger regardless of position (e.g. computing 6 − 3 instead of 13 − 6 in the ones place of 83 − 46). Using Dienes blocks to show that you cannot take 6 from 3 physically makes the need for regrouping concrete. Problems with zeros (803, 900) need an extra discussion: children may need to regroup twice.
materials: Dienes blocks or token sets per pair

section_titles: Problem Solving, Grid Hunt, and Missing Digits
periods.activity_title: Library Books, Train Stations, and Grid Hunts

tasks_in_class.description: Rami read Panchatantra Tales (236 pages); Kesu read Akbar Birbal, Karadi Tales, and Blue Umbrella. Who read more? How many more pages?
Train problem: how many passengers on the train when it leaves Dadri (after boarding 158, alighting 23, boarding 67, alighting 75 at stops)?
Find quick ways to solve: 326+25, 410−12, 675+5, 204−10, 811+99, 945−19 using strategies from Grade 3.
How many number pairs (adjacent vertically or horizontally) are there in the 4×4 grid?
Find the number pair in the grid whose sum is the greatest.

homework.description: Sumi has read 23 pages of Adventures of Feluda (128 pages). How many more pages are left?

time_bands.activity: Let Us Solve Q1a, p.110 ("who read more — Rami or Kesu? How many more pages?..."). Children first find Kesu's total by adding three book page-counts, then compare with Rami's 236. Pairs discuss the operation sequence before writing it down.

Let Us Solve Q2a, p.111 ("passengers on the train when it leaves Dadri...."). Children track passengers station by station, adding boarders and subtracting those alighting at each stop. Encourage a running-total table to organise the multi-step work.

Let Us Solve c, p.111 ("quick ways to solve 326+25, 410−12, 675+5, 204−10, 811+99, 945−19...."). Children share the mental strategy they used for each. Highlight that adding/subtracting a nearby round number and then adjusting is a useful shortcut.

Number Pair Hunt, p.112 ("count adjacent number pairs in the 4×4 grid....") and Number Pair Hunt Q1, p.113 ("find the pair with the greatest sum...."). Children work in pairs, circling adjacent pairs, then computing and comparing sums to find the largest.

periods.teacher_notes: For the multi-step library problem, children often add all page-counts without first reading who read which books; prompt careful reading of the table before operating. In the mental-strategy task, accept any valid strategy — decomposing addends, compensation, using multiples of 10 — and encourage children to articulate what they did, not just the answer.
materials: Board for recording running totals in the train problem
Book page-count data visible on board (from p.110 table)

section_titles: Problem Solving, Grid Hunt, and Missing Digits
periods.activity_title: Grid Extremes, Word Problems, and Missing Digits

tasks_in_class.description: Find the number pair in the grid whose sum is the smallest.
Find the number pair in the grid whose difference is the greatest.
Find the number pair in the grid whose difference is the smallest.
Fill the missing digits in 3 addition puzzles and 3 subtraction puzzles to make each sum correct.
Find two numbers whose sum is 856 and two numbers whose difference is 563; then make your own word problems with these numbers.

homework.book_ref: Let Us Solve a and b, p.111

time_bands.activity: Number Pair Hunt Q2–Q4, p.113 ("find pairs with smallest sum, greatest difference, smallest difference...."). Children continue with the same 4×4 grid, now searching for the remaining extremes. Pairs record each target pair and its computed result before comparing with another pair.

The Missing Digits, p.113 ("fill the missing digits in 3 addition and 3 subtraction puzzles...."). Children use reverse reasoning: if the ones column shows ☐ + 7 = 13, what is the missing digit? Work through one example together, then children attempt the remaining five independently.

Let Us Solve e, p.112 ("find two numbers whose sum is 856 and two numbers whose difference is 563...."). Children try multiple number pairs before settling on one, then compose a short word-problem context for each. Pairs share their word problems with the class.
Set homework: Let Us Solve a and b, p.111 — column addition 452+89 and subtraction 641−273.

periods.teacher_notes: In the Missing Digits task, children sometimes guess and check rather than reasoning from the known digit; prompt them to ask 'What must the ones digit be so that the ones column works?' before moving to tens. For the open sum/difference task, accept all valid pairs — there are many — and use the word-problem sharing to reinforce that the same numbers can tell very different stories.
materials: Grid from p.112–113 visible (board or textbook)

section_titles: Let Us Do — Mixed Addition and Subtraction Drill
periods.activity_title: Full-Range Drill: Adding and Subtracting with Confidence

time_bands.activity: Quick mental warm-up: teacher reads three addition and three subtraction expressions aloud; children write only the answer. This sets the pace for independent column work and surfaces any residual regrouping difficulties.

Let Us Do Q1, p.114 ("add: 23+489, 105+295, 630+56, 35+99, 409+387, 67+76, 580+207, 333+666, 826+268...."). Children work independently, aligning digits carefully. Encourage an estimate before each item to catch errors early. After individual work, children swap books and check the first four items with a partner.

Let Us Do Q2, p.114 ("subtract: 300−45, 962−268, 706−209, 842−387, 674−76, 754−409, 403−245, 600−384, 546−538...."). Children work independently. Circulate to assist with multiple regroupings (e.g. 600−384 requires regrouping from hundreds through tens). After individual work, selected answers are discussed on the board.

Class reflection: children identify one addition item and one subtraction item they found hardest, and explain in one sentence what made it tricky. This closes the drill with deliberate self-assessment.

periods.teacher_notes: Items with zeros (300−45, 706−209, 600−384) are consistently the hardest — children need to regroup across a zero and may freeze. Remind them to regroup the hundreds column first: 600 becomes 590+10 before the ones can be subtracted. The partner-checking habit built in the addition block transfers well to the subtraction block as self-monitoring.
materials: Board for working selected problems in full

items.prompt: Apples cost ₹40 per kg and oranges cost ₹30 per kg. Priya wants to spend exactly ₹130 on a mix of apples and oranges. Which combination can she buy?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 1 kg apples and 3 kg oranges: ₹40 + ₹90 = ₹130.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute the cost of each combination by multiplying quantity by price and adding the two amounts, then compare with ₹130.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student computes ₹80 + ₹30 = ₹110, not ₹130; likely forgot to multiply oranges correctly or used ₹30 once instead of per kg.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student computes ₹120 + ₹30 = ₹150, exceeding ₹130; may have reversed the search direction (started with more apples).
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student computes ₹80 + ₹60 = ₹140, close but over ₹130; indicates partial correct strategy but an arithmetic slip.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: try each option with play money; stretch: find a second combination that also totals ₹130.

exercise.description: Find costs for different quantities of fruits/vegetables; find what combinations sum to ₹163 (more than one possibility).

items.prompt: Mangoes cost ₹55 per kg. Raju wants to buy 3 kg of mangoes (total ₹165). He has one ₹100 note and three ₹20 notes. Can he pay the exact amount?

options.label: A
options.text: No, because ₹100 + three ₹20 notes = ₹160, which is less than ₹165

options.label: D
options.text: Yes, ₹100 + three ₹20 notes = ₹160, so he cannot pay exactly

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add the note values and compare the total with the required ₹165.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student correctly calculates ₹160 but then contradicts themselves by choosing 'Yes'; confusion between the result and the conclusion.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student incorrectly sums ₹100 + ₹60 as ₹165; likely an arithmetic error in adding three ₹20 notes.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student compares ₹100 alone with ₹165 without including the ₹20 notes; does not combine all currency.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: physically add the notes one at a time with play money; stretch: find a set of notes that does pay ₹165 exactly.

exercise.description: Lou and Daisy buy 3 kg bananas (₹165). Which of the currency options a–e can they use to pay?

items.prompt: Draw a triangle with 3 vertices and 3 midpoints (6 nodes total). Place the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 — each used once — so that the sum of the three numbers on each side of the triangle is 9. Write the number at each node.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: One valid arrangement: vertices 2, 4, 6 and midpoints 3, 5, 1 (placed so each side sums to 9). Multiple correct arrangements exist — accept any arrangement where all three side-sums equal 9 and each of 1–6 is used exactly once.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place larger numbers at midpoints and smaller numbers at vertices (or trial-and-adjust systematically) so each side of three nodes sums to 9.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: use numbered slips to physically move numbers until each side works; stretch: find a second different arrangement that also gives each side a sum of 9.

exercise.description: Place numbers 1–6 in triangle nodes so that the sum on each side is 9. No numbers repeated.

items.prompt: Using the numbers 1 to 6 each once in a magic triangle, which of these side-sums is NOT possible to achieve on all three sides at the same time?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 13 is not achievable. The achievable equal-side-sum values for numbers 1–6 in a magic triangle are 9, 10, 11, and 12.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Trial arrangement and checking: the maximum equal side-sum reachable with 1–6 is 12, so 13 cannot be achieved.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student believes 9 is impossible; they may not have found a valid arrangement yet — direct them to try placing 1, 2, 3 at vertices.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student believes 10 is impossible; they may have tried only one arrangement and not adjusted the vertex vs. midpoint positions.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student believes 11 is impossible; they likely stopped exploring at 9 and 10 and did not attempt higher sums.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: try building each sum with slips before answering; stretch: explain in one sentence why 13 cannot work.

exercise.description: What other sums can you make with these 6 numbers? Can you make 12 on each side? Can you make 13?

items.prompt: A class has 37 boys and 45 girls. Without adding exactly, which is the best estimate of the total number of children?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: About 80. Rounding 37 to 40 and 45 to 50 gives an estimate of 90; rounding both to the nearest ten gives 40 + 50 = 90, but the actual sum is 82, so 'about 80' is the closest reasonable estimate. Accept 80 or 90 if the child explains their rounding; 80 is the preferred answer as the exact sum is 82.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Round each number to the nearest ten, then add the rounded values to estimate.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student rounds 37 down to 30 and 45 down to 40, both rounding in the same direction and losing accuracy.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student rounds both numbers up (40 + 50 = 90); this is a reasonable estimate too, but 80 is closer to the actual answer of 82.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student overestimates significantly, possibly rounding 37 to 50 or 45 to 60; not a careful rounding.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write each number next to its nearest ten on a number line; stretch: compute the exact answer and compare it with both the 80 and 90 estimates, stating which is closer.

exercise.description: Estimate the number of teachers going on the trip (24 + 28) before computing.

items.prompt: A shopkeeper has 72 mangoes. She sells 38. Before computing exactly, which is the best estimate of how many mangoes are left?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: About 30. Rounding 72 to 70 and 38 to 40 gives 70 − 40 = 30. The exact answer is 34, so 30 is the closest estimate.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Round each number to the nearest ten and subtract to estimate.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may have rounded 72 to 70 and 38 to 50, over-rounding the subtrahend.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student rounded 72 up to 80 and 38 down to 40, giving 80 − 40 = 40; rounding in opposite directions inflates the estimate.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student likely subtracted tens only (70 − 30 = 40 or ignored the 8 altogether); did not account for rounding 38 up.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: mark 72 and 38 on a number line to see the gap before rounding; stretch: compute the exact answer and explain whether the estimate was too high or too low.

exercise.description: Estimate the difference: how many more children bought Pusaw than fruit plates (83 − 46)?

items.section_title: Problem Solving, Grid Hunt, and Missing Digits
items.prompt: Solve this quickly without column addition: 503 − 10. Write your answer and explain in one sentence how you found it without writing out the full column method.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 493. Subtracting 10 decreases the tens digit by 1 (5 tens becomes 4 tens), leaving the hundreds and ones unchanged.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recognise that subtracting 10 reduces only the tens digit by 1, with no regrouping needed.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: use a number line — hop back one group of 10 from 503; stretch: use the same strategy for 503 − 100 and explain the difference.

exercise.description: Find quick ways to solve: 326+25, 410−12, 675+5, 204−10, 811+99, 945−19 using strategies from Grade 3.

items.section_title: Problem Solving, Grid Hunt, and Missing Digits
items.prompt: Look at these four numbers: 120, 345, 89, 210. Which two adjacent numbers (placed next to each other in a row) give the greatest sum? Write the pair and their sum.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 345 and 210 give the greatest sum: 345 + 210 = 555.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the two largest adjacent values and add them.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: compute the sum of every adjacent pair and list them all; stretch: now find the adjacent pair with the greatest difference.

exercise.description: Find the number pair in the grid whose sum is the greatest.

items.section_title: Problem Solving, Grid Hunt, and Missing Digits
items.prompt: Look at these four numbers: 120, 345, 89, 210. Which two adjacent numbers give the greatest difference? Write the pair and their difference.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 345 and 89 give the greatest difference: 345 − 89 = 256.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify adjacent pairs, compute each difference, and select the largest.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: list all adjacent pairs (120–345, 345–89, 89–210) and compute each difference in turn; stretch: explain why 120 and 210 are not the answer even though they are further apart in value.

exercise.description: Find the number pair in the grid whose difference is the greatest.

items.section_title: Problem Solving, Grid Hunt, and Missing Digits
items.prompt:
Fill in the missing digit to make this addition correct:
  3 ☐ 5
+ 2 4 ☐
------
  6 0 3
What is the missing digit in the hundreds number's tens place, and what is the missing digit in the ones place of the second number?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Ones column: 5 + ☐ = 3 (with a carry of 1), so ☐ = 8 (since 5 + 8 = 13, write 3 carry 1). Tens column: ☐ + 4 + 1 (carry) = 0 (with a carry of 1), so ☐ = 5 (since 5 + 4 + 1 = 10, write 0 carry 1). Hundreds column: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 ✓. Missing tens digit of top number: 5. Missing ones digit of bottom number: 8.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Work column by column from ones to hundreds, using the known sum digit and any carry to find each missing digit.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: fill in the ones column first with a worked example alongside; stretch: create your own missing-digit puzzle for a partner to solve.

exercise.description: Fill the missing digits in 3 addition puzzles and 3 subtraction puzzles to make each sum correct.

items.section_title: Problem Solving, Grid Hunt, and Missing Digits
items.prompt: Find two numbers whose sum is 500. Write both numbers. Then write one sentence that makes a word problem using your two numbers and the sum 500.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any pair of whole numbers that add to 500 is correct (e.g. 250 and 250, or 300 and 200, or 375 and 125). The word problem must describe a real situation where two quantities combine to make 500.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Choose any number, subtract it from 500 to find the partner, then wrap the pair in a story context.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: start from 500 and count back by tens to find a partner; stretch: find three different pairs and write a word problem for the most interesting one.

exercise.description: Find two numbers whose sum is 856 and two numbers whose difference is 563; then make your own word problems with these numbers.

items.prompt: Add 367 + 248 using the column method with regrouping. What is the answer?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 615. Ones: 7 + 8 = 15, write 5 carry 1. Tens: 6 + 4 + 1 = 11, write 1 carry 1. Hundreds: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Align in H-T-O columns, add ones first with regrouping, then tens with regrouping, then hundreds.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student added correctly in tens and hundreds but missed adding the carry from the ones column to the tens column.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student may have computed 7 + 8 = 15 correctly but then added 6 + 4 = 10 without carrying from ones, giving tens digit 0 and hundreds 5+2+1=8; or another regrouping slip.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student correctly added the ones (5) and hundreds (6) but made a tens error: 6 + 4 = 10 written as 2 in tens place, suggesting they added 1+1 carry separately and got 12.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: use Dienes blocks to physically exchange 10 ones for 1 ten; stretch: try 467 + 358 independently.

items.prompt: Subtract 247 from 623 using the column method with regrouping. Write your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 376. Ones: 3 − 7 needs regrouping; borrow from tens → 13 − 7 = 6. Tens: (2−1) − 4 = 1 − 4 needs regrouping; borrow from hundreds → 11 − 4 = 7. Hundreds: (6−1) − 2 = 3.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Align in H-T-O columns, start from ones; regroup (exchange 1 ten for 10 ones, or 1 hundred for 10 tens) wherever the top digit is smaller than the bottom digit.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw tokens above each column to show regrouping physically; stretch: check the answer by adding 376 + 247 and confirming you get 623.

exercise.description: Subtract by aligning in columns: (a) 83−29 (b) 345−123 (c) 763−437 (d) 803−350 (e) 900−328.

items.section_title: Let Us Do — Mixed Addition and Subtraction Drill
items.prompt: Add 409 + 387. Write your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 796. Ones: 9 + 7 = 16, write 6 carry 1. Tens: 0 + 8 + 1 = 9. Hundreds: 4 + 3 = 7.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Column addition with regrouping from ones to tens; tens digit of first number is 0 so the carry from ones becomes the full tens contribution.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write 409 as 4 hundreds, 0 tens, 9 ones using the H-T-O grid before adding; stretch: estimate first, then verify your exact answer against your estimate.

items.section_title: Let Us Do — Mixed Addition and Subtraction Drill
items.prompt: Subtract: 600 − 384. Write your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 216. Ones: 0 − 4 needs regrouping; tens digit is also 0, so regroup from hundreds: 600 → 590 + 10; then 10 − 4 = 6. Tens: 9 − 8 = 1. Hundreds: 5 − 3 = 2.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: When both ones and tens digits of the top number are 0, regroup the hundred into 9 tens and 10 ones, then subtract column by column.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write 600 as 6 hundreds, 0 tens, 0 ones and use token diagrams to exchange 1 hundred for 10 tens and then 1 ten for 10 ones; stretch: subtract 385 from 600 and compare with this answer.

items.prompt: Meena buys vegetables costing ₹78. She pays with a ₹100 note. How much change does she receive?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract the cost from the amount paid to find the balance (change).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: use a number line to count up from ₹78 to ₹100; stretch: if Meena also buys fruit for ₹35 and pays with a ₹200 note, what change does she receive?

exercise.description: Complete 9 Cost–Paid–Balance grids by finding the missing value in each row.

items.section_title: A Strange Puzzle — Change from Oranges
items.prompt: Priya buys 2 bananas at ₹15 each. She pays with a ₹50 note. How much change does she get back?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: First find the total cost (2 × price), then subtract from the note paid to get the change.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw 2 bananas, write ₹15 under each, and add; stretch: how much change would she get if she paid with a ₹100 note instead?

exercise.description: Find the balance (paid amount minus ₹42) for Krishna (₹50), Sudama (₹100), Mala (₹200), and Neela (₹500).

items.prompt: A school library has 256 story books and 149 picture books. How many books are there in the library altogether?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 405. 256 + 149: ones 6 + 9 = 15, write 5 carry 1; tens 5 + 4 + 1 = 10, write 0 carry 1; hundreds 2 + 1 + 1 = 4.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add the two quantities in H-T-O columns with regrouping wherever a column sum reaches 10 or more.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: estimate first by rounding (256 ≈ 260, 149 ≈ 150, sum ≈ 410) to check reasonableness; stretch: 37 more picture books arrive — what is the new total?

exercise.description: 185 + 125: estimate the trip money, then write the final answer after regrouping in the H-T-O boxes.

items.prompt: One mango orchard has 315 trees. A nearby orchard has 246 more trees than the first orchard. How many trees does the nearby orchard have?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 561. 315 + 246: ones 5 + 6 = 11, write 1 carry 1; tens 1 + 4 + 1 = 6; hundreds 3 + 2 = 5.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Translate 'more than' as addition, then add in columns with regrouping from ones to tens.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a bar diagram — one bar for 315 and a longer bar for 315 + 246; stretch: how many trees are there in both orchards together?

exercise.description: Preeti's school has 423 children; cousin's school has 178 more. How many children study in Preeti's cousin's school?

items.prompt: A farmer harvested 614 coconuts this season and 375 last season. How many more coconuts did the farmer harvest this season than last season?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 239. 614 − 375: ones 4 − 5 needs regrouping → 14 − 5 = 9; tens (1−1) − 7 = 0 − 7 needs regrouping → 10 − 7 = 3; hundreds (6−1) − 3 = 2.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract in H-T-O columns starting from ones, regrouping wherever the top digit is smaller than the bottom digit.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: use token diagrams to show each regrouping step; stretch: check by adding 239 + 375 and confirming the result is 614.

exercise.description: Ram Chacha: 527 mangoes this year, 264 last year. Estimate then find how many more mangoes this year; use/draw tokens.

items.section_title: Problem Solving, Grid Hunt, and Missing Digits
items.prompt: A bookshelf has 3 shelves. The first shelf has 124 books, the second shelf has 98 books, and the third shelf has 115 books. How many books are on the bookshelf in total?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add the three quantities in two steps, regrouping where needed.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: add two shelves first and write the running total before adding the third; stretch: if 47 books are removed from the total, how many remain?

exercise.description: Rami read Panchatantra Tales (236 pages); Kesu read Akbar Birbal, Karadi Tales, and Blue Umbrella. Who read more? How many more pages?

items.section_title: Problem Solving, Grid Hunt, and Missing Digits
items.prompt: A bus starts its journey with 48 passengers. At the first stop, 15 passengers get off and 23 get on. At the second stop, 10 passengers get off and 8 get on. How many passengers are on the bus after the second stop?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Track passengers at each stop: subtract those alighting and add those boarding, in order.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a table with columns 'Start', 'Stop 1', 'Stop 2' and fill in the running total; stretch: how many passengers boarded the bus altogether across both stops?

exercise.description: Train problem: how many passengers on the train when it leaves Dadri (after boarding 158, alighting 23, boarding 67, alighting 75 at stops)?
